must_read.title: Metabolic Memory in Oral Inflammation
must_read.one_line: 综述表观遗传重编程驱动的代谢记忆如何维持口腔炎症持续与复发。
must_read.so_what: q1/q4可用：提供「宿主持久免疫编程」概念框架，指导种植体周炎转归与材料免疫编程研究设计。
must_read.caution: 纯综述，无新实验证据；需自行提炼可验证假说。
must_read.abstract: The global rise in metabolic diseases has increased the severity and therapeutic complexity of oral inflammatory disorders. Persistent inflammation driven by metabolic memory presents a central pathological mechanism. Even after metabolic parameters are normalized, abnormal gene expression can persist, leading to prolonged disease progression and recurrent episodes. In the oral cavity, metabolic memory is most clearly evident in periodontitis and impaired wound healing, where sustained immune dysregulation and tissue destruction remain after hyperglycemia or hyperlipidemia has been corrected. Epigenetic reprogramming presents a key molecular mechanism of metabolic memory, including DNA methylation, histone modifications, and expression of noncoding RNAs. The epigenetic alterations collectively reprogram immune cell function, driving the dysregulation of innate and adaptive immunity while influencing the fate of oral stromal cells and epithelial cells. Prolonged inflammation contributes to an altered host-microbiota interaction, reinforcing disease persistence and treatment resistance. Metabolic disorders induce coordinated epigenetic changes that can be grouped into permissive and repressive events affecting gene transcription. Permissive events include increased histone acetylation, enrichment of activating histone methylation marks (e.g., H3K4me3), and DNA demethylation at inflammatory gene loci. These modifications promote an open chromatin structure to enhance transcription factor access. Repressive events include increased DNA methylation and enrichment of repressive histone methylation marks (e.g., H3K9me3). DNA methylation typically occurs in promoter regions of genes, and repressive histone changes lead to the formation of compact chromatin, both of which reduce transcriptional activity. Noncoding RNAs generally decrease target messenger RNA stability or inhibit translation further, reinforcing a repressive effect. The combined effect of these modifications is a shift in protein expression that reinforces chronic inflammatory signaling in abnormal metabolic conditions. This review comprehensively summarizes the epigenetic mechanisms by which metabolic memory sustains oral inflammation at molecular, cellular, and tissue levels, as well as potential preventive and therapeutic interventions.

scan.title: Engineered synbiotic microspheres enable system-level reprogramming of the gut-immune-vascular axis in chronic inflammatory vascular disease
scan.title_zh: 工程合生元微球重编程肠-免疫-血管轴
scan.domain: 牙周炎通过哪些可验证的通…
scan.one_line: 工程化酶响应合生元微球递送益生菌、代谢抑制剂与益生元，重编程肠-免疫-血管轴逆转慢性炎症血管病。
scan.so_what: 系统水平轴重编程概念可借鉴；牙周炎-全身疾病通路设计参考。
scan.caution: 动物实验，人体转化未知；靶器官非口腔。
scan.abstract: Chronic inflammatory vascular diseases are increasingly recognized as systemic disorders sustained by maladaptive cross-organ immunometabolic coupling, yet current therapeutic strategies remain largely lesion-centered and fail to address upstream drivers of disease persistence. Here, we identify the gut-immune-vascular axis as a system-level pathogenic unit that integrates gut microbial dysbiosis, intestinal barrier dysfunction, metabolic imbalance, and vascular immune activation into a self-reinforcing pathological circuit. Through integrated clinical profiling and cross-species validation, we demonstrate that disruption of this axis is characterized by coordinated probiotic depletion, expansion of proinflammatory taxa, translocation of microbial endotoxins, accumulation of microbiota-derived metabolites, and macrophage polarization toward a proinflammatory phenotype along the gut-vascular continuum. To therapeutically target this axis, we engineer enzyme-responsive synbiotic microspheres that codeliver probiotics, a microbial metabolic pathway inhibitor, and a prebiotic within a protective polymeric matrix, enabling site-specific intestinal activation and coordinated microbiota-metabolic modulation. This engineered system restores intestinal barrier integrity, reprograms microbial ecology and metabolite output, suppresses immunometabolic dysfunction, and robustly attenuates pathological vascular remodeling across cellular, murine, and large-animal models, with in-stent restenosis serving as a representative disease context. Collectively, this work establishes axis-oriented immunometabolic reprogramming as a generalizable therapeutic paradigm and highlights engineered synbiotic platforms as scalable tools for system-level intervention in chronic inflammatory diseases.

scan.title: Regulatable membrane-bound IL-15 engineered TIL cell therapy for immune checkpoint inhibitor-resistant advanced melanoma: pooled analysis of phase 1 and 1/2 trials
scan.domain: 口腔鳞癌的免疫微环境与微…
scan.cluster: 口腔鳞癌的免疫微环境与微…
scan.abstract: Amsokigene autoleucel (amsoki-cel, OBX-115) is a tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) cell therapy engineered to express acetazolamide (ACZ)-regulatable membrane-bound interleukin-15, abrogating the need for interleukin-2. In two single-arm trials (completed phase 1 single-center first-in-human (FIH) and ongoing phase 1/2 multicenter Agni-01), patients with immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)-resistant advanced melanoma received lymphodepletion and varying doses and schedules of amsoki-cel and ACZ. The primary objective of FIH and Agni-01 phase 1 was safety, tolerability and recommended phase 2 dose (RP2D); the primary objective of Agni-01 phase 2 was objective response rate (ORR) at the RP2D. The first patient treated experienced rapid lymphocyte expansion and vasogenic edema of a previously irradiated brain metastasis, prompting protocol modifications and dose deescalation in FIH, including 80% reduction in maximum amsoki-cel dose and 75% reduction in ACZ dose. After preliminary demonstration of safety at the lower dose, doses were increased in FIH, and reescalation was initiated in Agni-01. Across studies, 37 patients were treated (FIH, n = 17; Agni-01, n = 20). Post hoc pooled analysis demonstrated no dose-limiting toxicities, ICU care or treatment-related mortality. Most common grade 3 or higher treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) included neutropenia (64.9% (24/37)), leukopenia/lymphopenia (56.8% (21/37) each) and anemia/thrombocytopenia (37.8% (14/37) each). Serious TEAEs were reported for 10 patients, including eight patients with grade 3 or higher events (non-hematologic, 13.5% (5/37); hematologic, 13.5% (5/37)). RP2D was selected based on overall safety and tolerability as well as preliminary anti-tumor activity in Agni-01 phase 1. The phase 2 preliminary ORR was 66.7% (6/9). In total, 15 patients were treated at RP2D and comprise the Key Efficacy Set (Agni-01: phase 1, n = 6; phase 2, n = 9), of which 10 patients (66.7%; 95% confidence interval 38-88%) achieved objective responses (including two complete responses). Amsoki-cel demonstrated favorable safety and promising early clinical activity in patients with ICI-resistant melanoma. A separate phase 2 pivotal Agni-01 cohort is ongoing. ClinicalTrials.gov identifiers: NCT05470283 and NCT06060613 .

scan.title: Exploring Community-Based Oral Health Screening and Prevention for Children, With Children, in Non-Clinical Settings: An Explanatory Parallel Mixed Methods Study
scan.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Lack of regular access to dental services for children can increase disease prevalence and burden on NHS services, which is aggravated for the most vulnerable. Non-clinical community hubs could be a feasible alternative for dental checks and oral health education. The aim of this study was to assess the oral health of children attending a non-clinical community hub, and the feasibility/acceptability of these settings to children. METHOD: This study adopted an parallel mixed-methods approach. Dental screening of children (0-16 years old) was undertaken in a non-clinical community hub by a trained and calibrated dentist in April 2024. Basic demographics, global quality of life and clinical data were collected. All children were given oral health education using tooth models and dietary advice. A sub-sample of children were recruited for qualitative inquiry, using a purposive sampling strategy. Three focus groups were facilitated with a pre-determined topic guide and creative arts-based techniques to facilitate discussion. These were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim and inductively coded following thematic analysis. RESULTS: Over the 5-day period, 141 children were screened with a mean age of 6.4 years (SD 3.8). Mean d3mft was 1.7 (SD 2.9; 0-15), D3MFT was 0.3 (SD 0.9; 0-4), and combined d3mft/D3MFT was 2.0 (SD 3.1; 0-19). Fifteen patients had silver diamine fluoride, 125 had fluoride varnish and one refused. Forty-one children were signposted for future care. Three focus groups involving 11 children identified three themes that were constructed from the data were: 'space' requirements; promoting positive engagement; familiarity with the environment. Children were generally accepting of foodbanks as settings for oral health screening and preventive care. They emphasised the importance of child-friendly, non-threatening spaces and highlighted how familiar environments and trusted staff fostered feelings of safety and engagement. CONCLUSION: Non-clinical community hubs are feasible and acceptable spaces to children to screen for oral health, providing a unique opportunity to reduce barriers to access and to target underserved groups with following on screening activities.
